title: Kirtan in new places
hook: hymns now sound in gurdwaras on every continent, in old ragas and new voices

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second generation: Saturday Gurmukhi classes, Punjabi at home, and your line, two worlds, one heart. Today, the thing that sounds the same in both worlds: the Guru's song. Day three hundred twenty-four.

Somewhere in the world, right now, someone is singing the Guru's hymns. Early morning in Amritsar, the kirtan at the Harmandir Sahib has already begun. In Nairobi, a family is gathering. In Vancouver it's night, and a teenager is practicing on a harmonium, wearing headphones so she won't wake her little brother. In a gurdwara in Kuala Lumpur, a group of old men is singing along with a tabla. Follow the sun around the planet, and the song never stops. Today: kirtan in new places.
screen: `SOMEONE IS SINGING RIGHT NOW.` → `AMRITSAR, NAIROBI, VANCOUVER.` → `THE SONG NEVER STOPS.`

segments.voice: Kirtan means singing the praise of God, and for Sikhs it means singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib. It began with Guru Nanak and his companion Bhai Mardana, a Muslim musician who played the rabab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the start, the Guru's word was meant to be sung. That's why the Guru Granth Sahib is arranged not by author or subject, but by raag: musical modes, each with its own mood and time of day. There are thirty-one main raags in it. Some are for dawn, some for evening, some for longing, some for joy. Over the centuries, the instruments changed. The harmonium, brought to India by Europeans in the 1800s, became the most common sound in gurdwaras. Recently, many young musicians have gone back to the old stringed instruments the Gurus' musicians played: the rabab, the dilruba, the taus. So kirtan today is both: old raags, and new voices. The diaspora has carried it everywhere. Kirtan now sounds in gurdwaras on every continent, in classrooms and camps, on phones and livestreams. The kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast every day, so a grandmother in England can listen along with Amritsar at breakfast. Children learn the tabla in the same gurdwaras where their parents learned to read Gurmukhi. And people who aren't Sikh often find they love it too, even before they understand a word. The Gurus taught that the Name is sung, not only studied. And now that song is everywhere.
screen: `NANAK SINGS, MARDANA PLAYS.` · `ARRANGED BY RAAG, NOT BY AUTHOR.` · `HARMONIUM, AND OLD STRINGS REVIVED.` · `EVERY CONTINENT, EVERY SCREEN.` · then, large: `THE SONG EVERYWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to kirtan from far away. If you can, find a recording of kirtan, or the live broadcast from the Harmandir Sahib, and play it softly. If you can't right now, remember any kirtan you've heard on this path. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to follow the words. Just let the sound come to you from far away, the way it reaches millions of people every day. Let it hold your attention. When your mind wanders, come back to the sound. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan in new places. The Guru's hymns, sung in old raags and new voices, now sound in gurdwaras and homes on every continent.
Your line: the song everywhere. Today, when you hear music, remember that somewhere on earth, right now, someone is singing the Guru's hymns. Day three hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Kirtan is sung in every gurdwara, usually with harmonium and tabla, and more and more with stringed instruments; the kirtan from the Harmandir Sahib is broadcast daily for Sikhs around the world.
